Buying well

Twelve questions to ask before you choose an installer

The questions that separate a considered proposal from a sales pitch — and the answers that should make you pause.

Published 28 September 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Most disputes in residential solar come down to expectations that were never written down: what the system would generate, what the savings would be, who handles a warranty claim, and what happens if something fails. These questions are designed to surface those expectations before you sign.

On the design

  1. What are you basing the system size on — my actual usage data, or an assumption? A serious proposal references your consumption, not a standard package.
  2. What generation do you expect, and what assumptions produced that figure? Ask for the specific yield assumption.
  3. How will the system be laid out, and what happens with shading? Ask what time of day shading affects each plane.
  4. What happens to my daytime surplus — self-consumed, stored, or exported at what rate?

On the equipment

  1. Exactly which panel, inverter and battery models are quoted, and why those? Model numbers, not brand names.
  2. What are the warranty terms, including whether labour is covered and who you contact first? Manufacturer warranties and installer workmanship warranties are different things.
  3. Is the inverter hybrid-capable, or would a battery later require additional equipment?

On the paperwork and compliance

  1. What documentation will I receive at handover? Expect certificates of electrical safety where required, compliance paperwork, monitoring access and product documentation.
  2. How are incentives handled in the price, and what happens if the value changes before installation?
  3. What grid approvals are needed in my area, who lodges them, and how long do they take?

On the after-sales reality

  1. What does monitoring show me, and who reviews it if output drops?
  2. If a component fails in year four, what is the process and the typical timeframe?

Answers that should give you pause

A guaranteed savings figure with no assumptions. A promise that you will definitely receive a rebate. Pressure to sign today to lock in a price or a program. No written specification. Refusal to put generation assumptions in writing. A quote that is dramatically cheaper than every other quote for an identical specification.

A practical comparison method

Put each quote into the same four-column table: specification (panel, inverter, battery, mounting, monitoring), expected generation with its assumption, installed price and incentive treatment, and warranty and service terms. Compare the tables, not the brochures. Where a quote cannot fill in a column, that is itself information.

Finally, check accreditation directly with the relevant industry body or program list rather than relying on a logo in a proposal, and confirm that any product quoted appears on the eligible product list for the program whose support is included in the price.

Key takeaways

  • Demand consumption-based reasoning, model numbers and written assumptions.
  • Warranties come in layers — workmanship, product, performance — and the quote should name who covers what.
  • Incentive treatment and its conditions belong in writing, including what happens if values change.
  • Guaranteed savings figures and signing pressure are warnings, not features.
  • Compare specification tables, not brochures — and verify accreditation independently.
